summary: This document defines a collection of common data types in the YANG data modeling language. They are designed to be imported by other YANG modules written in the routing area, so each module does not have to redefine them.

plainLanguage.summary: YANG is the language used to describe the configuration and state of network equipment, so that a management system can read it and a device can be told what to do. When several such descriptions need the same kind of value, such as a route target or a timer, they tend to define it separately and end up with different names and formats for the same thing. This RFC collects the common ones into two shared modules that other modules can import.

subtitle: A shared set of YANG data types so routing modules stop each inventing their own.

tldr.problem: Network management models written in YANG keep redefining the same things. A router identifier, a route target, a route distinguisher, a timer, a percentage: each module that needs one tends to define its own, with its own name, range and formatting rules.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines two YANG modules of derived types. The IETF module, ietf-routing-types, holds the common routing types that do not correspond directly to an IANA registry entry, such as router identifiers, route targets, multicast addresses, timers and MPLS labels. The IANA module, iana-routing-types, holds the types that mirror IANA registries, and IANA maintains that module itself.
tldr.outcome: Other routing modules import these types instead of writing their own, so the same value is spelled the same way everywhere. The RFC also fixes the exact ranges and text patterns, and provides groupings for label stacks and VPN route target rules that other modules can reuse whole.

today: RFC 8294 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2017, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the general YANG types in RFC 6991 and on the YANG 1.1 language in RFC 7950.

sections.title: Why a Shared Set of Types
sections.content:
YANG is a data modeling language used to model configuration data, state data, Remote Procedure Calls and notifications for network management protocols. The language supports a small set of built-in data types and provides mechanisms to derive other types from the built-in types.

This document introduces a collection of common data types derived from the built-in YANG types, designed to be the common types applicable for modelling in the routing area. The point is that a module written for one routing protocol should not have to invent its own version of a router identifier or a timer, because the result is that the same value is spelled differently in different places, and a management system has to understand several spellings of the same thing.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG has only a handful of built-in types, so everything else has to be derived from them. The usual practice has been for each protocol's module to derive its own version of the same concepts. This RFC derives the ones that routing protocols keep needing, once, in a way everyone can import.

sections.title: What the Two Modules Contain
sections.content:
The document defines two YANG modules for common routing types. The only module imports are from RFC 6991, namely ietf-yang-types and ietf-inet-types. The ietf-routing-types module contains the common routing types other than those corresponding directly to IANA mappings. These include router identifiers, which are commonly used to identify nodes in routing and other control-plane protocols; route targets, which are commonly used to control the distribution of Virtual Routing and Forwarding information in support of BGP/MPLS IP VPNs and BGP/MPLS Ethernet VPNs; IPv6 route targets, which are IPv6 Address Specific BGP Extended Communities and are 20 octets including an IPv6 address as the global administrator; route target types, which define the import and export rules of route targets; route distinguishers, which are commonly used to identify separate routes in support of VPNs; route origins and IPv6 route origins; the IPv4 and IPv6 multicast group and source address types; bandwidth in IEEE 754 floating-point 32-bit binary format, which is commonly used in traffic engineering control-plane protocols; the IGP link type; timer values and timer multipliers; a percentage; a 64-bit timeticks type; a 24-bit unsigned integer; and the Generalized Label, special-purpose MPLS label and general-use MPLS label types.

The module also defines two groupings: mpls-label-stack, a reusable collection of schema nodes representing an MPLS label stack, and vpn-route-targets, a reusable collection representing the route target import and export rules used in BGP-enabled VPNs.

The iana-routing-types module contains the common routing types that correspond directly to IANA mappings: address-family, whose values are based on the IANA Address Family Numbers registry, and subsequent-address-family, whose values are based on the IANA Subsequent Address Family Identifiers registry.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two modules. One holds the things that routing protocols invent for themselves, such as route targets and timers. The other holds the things that simply mirror a list IANA keeps, such as the address family numbers. Anything else a module needs, it derives itself.

sections.title: How the Types Are Defined
sections.content:
The derived types are defined with the same machinery YANG provides for any type. A router identifier is a 32-bit number in dotted-quad format assigned to each router, which uniquely identifies the router within an Autonomous System. A route target is a string matching one of several patterns: an 8-octet BGP extended community that initially identified a set of sites in a BGP VPN but has since taken on a more general role in BGP route filtering, consisting of a 2-octet type field, an administrator field and optionally an assigned number field. The defined formats are 2-octet-AS-number with a 4-octet number, 4-octet IPv4 address with a 2-octet number, 4-octet-AS-number with a 2-octet number, and 6-octet MAC address, with a generic pattern defined for future types. Valid examples given are 0:100:100, 1:1.1.1.1:100, 2:1234567890:203 and 6:26:00:08:92:78:00.

The numeric ranges are fixed rather than left open. The general-use MPLS label covers the 20-bit label value in an MPLS label stack, excluding the special-purpose values and excluding the encodings of Traffic Class and TTL, and its range is 16 to 1048575. The special-purpose MPLS label type is an identity reference, so that the well-known labels such as the IPv4 Explicit NULL, the IPv6 Explicit NULL, the Router Alert, the Implicit NULL, the Entropy Label Indicator, the Generic Associated Channel Label, the OAM Alert Label and the Extension Label are named rather than numbered. The mpls-label type is the union of the two. The 24-bit unsigned integer covers 0 to 16777215, and the percentage covers 0 to 100.

The timer types are unions: a numeric range together with two extra values, infinity and not-set, so that a timer can be switched off or left unset. timer-value-seconds16 covers 1 to 65535 seconds, timer-value-seconds32 covers 1 to 4294967295 seconds, and timer-value-milliseconds covers 1 to 4294967295 milliseconds. The timer multiplier is an 8-bit unsigned integer giving the number of timer intervals that should be interpreted as a failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Every type here states its range exactly. A route target is a string in one of four named shapes, and the RFC gives examples of each. A label has a stated numeric range, with the well-known special labels named separately rather than numbered. A timer is a number with two extra values, infinity and not-set, so that a timer can be turned off.

sections.title: The IANA-Maintained Module
sections.content:
The iana-routing-types module is intended to reflect the IANA Address Family Numbers registry and the Subsequent Address Family Identifiers registry. IANA has added a note to its own registry saying that address families and subsequent address families must not be directly added to the module, but must instead be added to the two registries, and that when the module is updated a new revision statement must be added in front of the existing revision statements.

When an address family or subsequent address family is added to the corresponding registry, a new enum statement must be added to the module. The name of the enum is the same as the corresponding address family or SAFI, except that it is a valid YANG identifier in all lowercase with hyphens separating the words in a compound name. The enum carries the IANA-assigned value, a status of deprecated or obsolete when a registration has been retired, a description replicated from the registry, and a reference replicated from the registry with the title of the document added. Unassigned or reserved values are not present in the module.
sections.plainLanguage: The second module is a mirror of two IANA lists, and IANA keeps the mirror up to date. New entries go into the IANA registry first, and the module gains a matching enumerated value. Values that are merely unassigned do not appear at all.

sections.title: Registrations
sections.content: The document registers two namespace URIs in the IETF XML Registry: urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-routing-types, with the IESG as registrant contact, and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:iana-routing-types, with IANA as registrant contact. It also registers the two YANG module names in the YANG Module Names registry: ietf-routing-types with the prefix rt-types, and iana-routing-types with the prefix iana-rt-types, both referencing this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Each module gets a permanent name and a short prefix that other modules use when they refer to its types, so that the definitions have one well-known identity.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document defines common routing type definitions, that is typedef statements, using the YANG data modeling language. The definitions themselves have no security or privacy impact on the Internet, but the usage of these definitions in concrete YANG modules might have. The security considerations spelled out in the YANG 1.1 specification apply for this document as well.
sections.plainLanguage: A list of type definitions has no security impact by itself. What matters is how the modules that import these types use them, and the YANG specification's own security guidance applies to those modules.

items.title: The registry comes first
items.text: Address families and subsequent address families are added to the IANA registries, never straight into the module.

items.title: One enum per entry
items.text: Each new registry entry gains a matching enum, named in lowercase with hyphens between the words.

items.title: Value, status and text
items.text: The enum carries the IANA-assigned value, a status of deprecated or obsolete when retired, and the registry's own description and reference.

items.title: No gaps
items.text: Unassigned or reserved values are not present in the module at all.

items.title: A new revision each time
items.text: Every update adds a new revision statement in front of the existing ones.
